Malaria risk is negligible. Travel insurance advice: EU citizens should carry EHIC for access to public healthcare. All other visitors should have comprehensive travel health insurance. Private hospitals are significantly better and require payment upfront.

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Honey Trap Bar Scam (nightlife, severity: high). You're walking near the ruin bars when an attractive woman strikes up a friendly conversation and suggests you grab a drink together at a nearby bar she knows. The evening seems great — until the bill arrives for €500 to €5,000 for a few drinks. The bar is in on it, bouncers block the exit, and victims have reported being forced to make ATM withdrawals. This is one of Budapest's most serious and well-documented scams. How to avoid: Never follow strangers to bars they choose — pick your own or go to established ruin bars Check prices before ordering anything and see a written menu If you're handed a massive bill, know that many victims have successfully refused to pay and left — call the police if needed

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Taxi Price Gouging (transport, severity: high). You hail a taxi outside a popular area and the driver mentions a 'special tourist rate' or the meter runs at triple speed. Some drivers take elaborate routes while the meter ticks up. Victims have been charged €50-100 for trips that should cost €10-15. Unofficial 'fake taxi' drivers also operate near the airport and party district. How to avoid: Only use Bolt (most popular app in Budapest) or licensed taxi companies like City Taxi Never get into an unmarked taxi Fares from airport to city center should be around 7,000-9,000 HUF

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — ATM Currency Conversion Trap (DCC) (money, severity: moderate). You use an ATM and it asks whether you want to complete the transaction in your home currency (e.g., USD/EUR) or in Hungarian Forints. The screen makes it seem like choosing your home currency is the helpful option. In reality, choosing your home currency activates Dynamic Currency Conversion — a terrible exchange rate that costs 5-15% more than letting your bank convert it. How to avoid: Always choose to pay/withdraw in local currency (Hungarian Forints) Use ATMs attached to actual banks rather than standalone machines Decline DCC at every ATM and card terminal in Hungary

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Restaurant Bill Inflation (overcharging, severity: moderate). You sit down at a traditional Hungarian restaurant and order goulash and palinka. When the bill comes, it includes items you didn't order — bread, amuse-bouche, service charges — that weren't mentioned or priced on the menu. Some restaurants also charge extra for table service, bring unsolicited items, or pad the receipt with mysterious line items. How to avoid: Ask to see a full menu with prices before sitting down Send back any food you didn't order before touching it Ask for itemized receipt and compare to menu prices before paying

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Fake Transport Pass Online (transport, severity: moderate). Before your trip, you find what appears to be BKK's (Budapest public transport) official Facebook page advertising discounted travel passes. The deal looks great — a 7-day pass for half price. You pay, receive a confirmation, but the pass either never arrives or is counterfeit and gets rejected at barriers. The Facebook page is a fake impersonating the real BKK. How to avoid: Only buy BKK passes from official BKK apps, official website, or station ticket offices Check the URL carefully — official site is bkk.hu If the deal seems too cheap to be real, it almost certainly is

Scam alert in Budapest, Hungary — Friendly Stranger Chess Game Hustle (distraction, severity: low). A friendly older man challenges you to a game of chess in the park, claiming it's a local tradition. He seems casual and friendly, and the stakes start small. But he's a skilled hustler who loses early on purpose, raises the stakes, and before you know it you're down €20-50 and he suddenly becomes much better at chess. It's a long-con version of street gambling. How to avoid: Only play games with strangers in formal public settings Never bet money in informal street games Enjoy watching chess in the park but decline to play for money

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Port Gruž Cruise-Taxi Overcharge (overcharging, severity: high). A taxi rank positioned immediately outside Port Gruž cruise terminal funnels disembarking passengers into unmetered cars at flat €40–80 fares for Old Town runs that should cost €12–20 metered. A British cruise passenger on Tripadvisor (Jun 7, 2024) was charged €55 for a 15-minute Gruž-to-Old Town ride where Uber was quoting €12. The Dubrovnik Times (Aug 9, 2025) reported an unlicensed driver hid his plates with garbage bags to enter Dubrovnik's Special Traffic Management Zone; the mayor proposed amending the Road Transport Act in Sep 2025. Transport Minister Oleg Butković announced on Nova TV Dnevnik (Aug 28, 2025) that fare caps would be reintroduced in response to Split and Dubrovnik cases. Cruise Critic's 'Dubrovnik late afternoon Taxi scams' thread documents the return-to-ship window specifically. How to avoid: Open Uber or Bolt before leaving the ship — both operate legally in Dubrovnik and show the full fare up front (the US State Department Croatia advisory explicitly recommends them). Take Libertas bus 1A or 1B from Gruž to Pile Gate for €2, or the cruise shuttle if your line offers one. Photograph the taxi's plate, the driver's ID, and the meter before loading luggage. Pay by card with a receipt showing the company's business registration number; refuse cash-only drivers. Report overcharges to 112 (EU emergency) or the Dubrovnik-Neretva Police on +385 20 443 333 within 48 hours. Dubrovnik Tourist Board at Brsalje 5, +385 20 312 011, handles Tourism Quality Service complaints.

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Old Town Menu Bait-and-Switch (overcharging, severity: moderate). Old Town restaurants on Stradun, Prijeko and Od Puča post the cheapest item on a chalkboard outside, then hand you a menu 2–3× more expensive once you are seated. Anchor prices inside the walls: €5 for a scoop of gelato, €25+ for a seafood pasta, €6 for a coffee on the Stradun (Croatia Travel Facebook group, 2024 Viralsnare investigation). A 2024 Tripadvisor thread walks through the mechanic at Korta Bistro & Wine Bar just off Stradun. The Medium piece 'The Terrible Story Of How I Got Scammed In Dubrovnik' documents 70 kuna (~€9.30) for a single juice with menu-swap photos. Traveler reports summarize the post-euro picture. Three moves: different chalkboard vs table menu; seafood 'market price by the kilogram' with no weight disclosed (whole sea bass €60–90); and cover charges (coperto) of €3–5 per person in small type at the bottom of the bill. How to avoid: Eat outside the walls — Lapad, Gruž, Ploče — where prices are half and the food is often better. Ask for the English menu with printed prices before you order; photograph the chalkboard menu in the alley next to your table number. For seafood, always confirm price per kilogram and the final total in euros before the fish goes to the grill. Pay by card for chargeback recourse. For disputes, call the Croatian Ministry of Finance consumer hotline 072 213 213, Dubrovnik-Neretva Police on 112 or +385 20 443 333, and Dubrovnik Tourist Board on +385 20 312 011.

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Fake Apartment & Booking.com Reservation Hijack (identity-theft, severity: high). A 26-year-old Slovak tourist lost €1,050 in March 2025 to a fake Dubrovnik rental advertised on what looked like a legitimate booking site (Dubrovnik Times, Mar 18, 2025). The Polish embassy in Zagreb has publicly warned its citizens about scammers publishing the same Dubrovnik apartment under several names and prices on Booking.com to trigger overbookings (TVP World, 2024). The BBC's Nov 2024 'reservation hijacking' story documents the data-breach pattern: leaked guest bookings sent to criminals who WhatsApp the target impersonating the hotel and demand a 'card verification' payment. Three mechanic versions: cloned-listing (scammer copies a real apartment to Instagram/Marketplace or phishing domain, takes €500–1,500 SEPA transfer and disappears); reservation-hijack (WhatsApp credential phish after legitimate Booking.com booking); and overbooking (same apartment listed three or four times on Booking.com at different prices, first tourist through the door keeps it). Slobodna Dalmacija's Neum fake-villa exposé shows the pattern targets the broader Dalmatian coast. How to avoid: Book only through the official Booking.com, Airbnb, or Vrbo app — never through an email link — and ignore any request for card verification or payment outside the platform, regardless of the logo on the message. Pay only on arrival, keys in hand. Cross-check apartment addresses in the Croatian eVisitor tourism registry and host names at sudreg.pravosudje.hr (both free). Use a credit card with chargeback rights; never pay by SEPA before arrival. For losses, call Dubrovnik-Neretva Police on +385 20 443 333, your card fraud line within 30 days, and Croatian Ombudsman +385 1 49 21 837. US Embassy Zagreb +385 1 661 2200, UK Embassy Zagreb +385 1 6009 100 for emergency accommodation referrals.

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — City Walls & Dubrovnik Pass Fake-Ticket Resellers (counterfeit, severity: moderate). The official Dubrovnik City Walls ticket is €35 adults in 2025 (or bundled into the €40 Dubrovnik Pass from dubrovnikpass.com), but third-party resellers sell the same ticket at €45–70 with a 'skip-the-line' label that does not skip anything — and a parallel ecosystem of phishing websites charges your card and emails an unusable voucher. A canonical Tripadvisor review ('SCAM — use official site Dubrovnik Pass,' on Gulliver Travel) records €50 per person; a Viator 'Skip-the-Line Dubrovnik Cable Car' review logs €92 vs €52 at the counter. The Srđ Cable Car official return ticket is €27 at the Petra Krešimira IV lower terminus. Three mechanic versions: phishing domains like 'dubrovnikcitywalls.com' that take card and email a QR that fails at Pile Gate; legitimate-but-marked-up OTA listings at 20–100% above counter; and street touts at Pile and Brsalje selling already-used tickets or laminated cards the gate does not recognize. How to avoid: Buy City Walls and Old Town monument tickets at dubrovnikpass.com (Dubrovnik Tourist Board's own portal) or at the Pile Gate, Ploče Gate, or St. John's Fort ticket booths on the day — there is no meaningful 'skip-the-line' option. Buy Srđ Cable Car tickets at dubrovnikcablecar.com or the Petra Krešimira IV lower terminus counter. Refuse street touts — Croatian law requires licensed tour operators to wear a visible Ministry of Tourism badge with a license number. For phishing losses, call your card issuer's 24-hour fraud line, file at Dubrovnik-Neretva Police on +385 20 443 333, and call the Croatian Ministry of Finance consumer hotline 072 213 213.

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Fake-QR-Code Parking Meter (identity-theft, severity: moderate). In July 2025, Dubrovnik police discovered scammers had pasted stickers with fake QR codes over legitimate codes on parking meters across the city. Tourists scanning them were routed to a phishing page that captured card details instead of paying for parking; the City of Dubrovnik peeled dozens of stickers off, per traveler reports. Drivers who thought they had 'paid' still got tickets while losing card numbers, expiry, CVV, and 3-D Secure codes. An older Tripadvisor 'Be Aware of Parking Scam' thread from the Pile / cable-car lower-terminus car park documents an adjacent pattern — fake high-vis 'attendants' demanding cash for 'parking' on streets where parking is actually metered. Separately, MSN documents a Dalmatian-coast SMS parking-phishing variant in which tourists receive a 'unpaid ticket' text with a payment link after the fact. How to avoid: Pay Dubrovnik parking only via the official Sanitat payDo+ app (Apple App Store / Google Play) or coin/card directly at the meter's physical interface — do not scan roadside QR codes unless you have verified the URL against the printed domain on the meter. Verify any URL shows sanitat.hr or dubrovnik.hr before entering card details. If you already entered details into a suspect QR site, block your card immediately with your issuer and call Dubrovnik-Neretva Police +385 20 443 333. Legitimate Dubrovnik tickets are paper on the windscreen — ignore post-trip SMS/WhatsApp/email 'unpaid parking ticket' messages, which are phishing. Dubrovnik Tourist Board at Brsalje 5, +385 20 312 011.

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Unlicensed Elafiti & Game of Thrones Tour Operator (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). 'Private' Elafiti boat tours advertised at €400 turn into shared tours with a curtain at the dock, unlicensed skippers offer 'Game of Thrones island hopping' without Croatian maritime insurance, and firsthand Tripadvisor reports document repeated no-show bookings. Three canonical firsthand case files: 'AVOID TRITON. SCAM' on Dubrovnik Boat Excursions (Elafiti private-to-shared switch); 'Super Tours: Tourist scam and overpriced' (Pile Gate GoT island tours); 'Mala Mara: THIS IS A FRAUDULENT BUSINESS AND A SCAM' (Aug 8, 2025 no-show with disputed refund). The Gari Transfer operator guide codifies the three moves: 'private boat = shared with a curtain,' unlicensed boat without safety certification, and bait-and-switch pricing (€400 becomes €550 at the dock). Ministry of Tourism requires licensed tour guides to wear a numbered badge; Pile Gate touts in branded T-shirts are reliably unlicensed. How to avoid: Book island tours through Krilo, Jadrolinija, Dubrovnik Boat Trips (dubrovnikboattrips.com), or OTAs with 1,000+ reviews (GetYourGuide's Elaphite Island Cruise has 4,570+ reviews). For Game of Thrones tours, only book guides displaying a Ministry of Tourism badge with license number — the Dubrovnik Tourist Guides Association at Brsalje 5 (+385 20 312 011) keeps the list. Check VAT number and tax-registered receipt before paying. Never pay more than 30% up front; pay the remainder by card on arrival. For disputes, call the Harbour Master's Office +385 20 418 988 and Dubrovnik-Neretva Police +385 20 443 333.

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Stradun Currency Exchange & Euronet ATM Markup (overcharging, severity: moderate). Since Croatia adopted the euro on January 1, 2023, currency exchange has become a smaller problem but ATM dynamic-currency-conversion (DCC) markups at independent Euronet machines have filled the gap. Traveler reports describe Euronet as 'rip-off' and 'scam machines' offering exchange rates 20–25% worse than major Croatian banks; the Adriatic 'is full of nobody's ATMs with brutal [fees]' per a 2025 traveler report. Paul Bradbury's widely-shared 2024 Facebook post estimates Euronet commissions at 20–25%. The Dubrovnik Times reports EU payment fraud up 43% in 2024 (European Banking Authority). The Split Tourist Board's own article documents tourists receiving 610 kuna for €100 at a booth instead of the legitimate 730–740. Two mechanics: ATM DCC (Euronet/Cashzone/Your Cash defaults the 'accept conversion' button 5–15% worse than your bank rate, plus €4–8 withdrawal fees); and booth exchange with hidden commission of up to 15% in small print. How to avoid: Use only ATMs on the outer wall of a named Croatian bank — Zagrebačka Banka on Stradun, Privredna Banka at Pile Gate, Erste on Obala Stjepana Radića in Gruž, OTP near Ploče. Always decline DCC; choose 'Pay in EUR' / 'Charge without conversion.' Your home bank converts at a far better rate. Withdraw larger amounts less often to minimise per-transaction fees. For manual exchange use a named Croatian-bank branch rather than a street booth. For card fraud call your issuer first, then +385 20 443 333 (Police), +385 1 49 21 837 (Ombudsman), and 072 213 213 (Ministry of Finance consumer hotline).

Scam alert in Dubrovnik, Croatia — Stradun & City Walls Pickpocket Window (pickpocket, severity: moderate). Pickpocketing inside the walls is concentrated in two predictable compressions — Pile Gate and the viewpoint benches on the City Walls during the mid-day cruise-ship wave. The UK FCDO Croatia safety advisory (2025) explicitly names Split and Dubrovnik as places where 'pickpockets operate in tourist areas.' The Bookiscout Dubrovnik Safety Guide 2026 pins the hottest window: 'Stradun (Placa)... especially from 10:00 AM to 2:00 PM.' Three architectural hotspots: Pile Gate is a single stone arch about three metres wide channelling the entire cruise-ship tide onto Stradun; the City Walls circuit is 1.94 km with viewpoint benches at Minčeta Tower and St. John's Fort where people set bags down to photograph; and the Buža Gate cliff-side bar at sunset with its dark setting and distracting view. The US State Department summarizes: 'Violent crime is rare. Petty crime cases have been reported in densely-populated tourist areas.' Crime tends to be opportunistic rather than organized-group. How to avoid: Wear bags crossbody with the zipper against your chest; keep phone in a zipped front pocket, never a back pocket or the outer mesh pouch of a backpack. At Pile Gate and Ploče Gate, briefly turn your backpack to your front as you pass through the arch. On the City Walls, keep your bag on your lap when you sit on a viewpoint bench. At Buža Gate's cliff bar, keep your phone off the stone bench. Carry only one card and €100–200 in cash; leave the rest in the hotel safe. For thefts, call 112 or 192 (Police) immediately and file at Dubrovnik-Neretva Police on +385 20 443 333. Dubrovnik Tourist Board at Brsalje 5, +385 20 312 011, has a walk-in desk for incident-report referrals.

Scam alert in Krakow, Poland — The Strip Club Honeytrap (nightlife, severity: high). You're wandering near the Cloth Hall after a few drinks when an attractive woman makes eye contact and suggests you all go somewhere fun together. She leads you and your group to a 'club' down a side street where you're ushered to a table. Hours later, the bill arrives: €500 per person for drinks that were never priced on the menu. When you refuse, bouncers appear. This is Krakow's most documented tourist scam — traveler reports number in the hundreds, and many involve drugged drinks and forced ATM withdrawals. How to avoid: Never follow strangers to clubs in Old Town Only go to venues you researched beforehand Use Booking.com/Google Maps to find reputable bars If you end up somewhere sketchy, leave before ordering

Scam alert in Krakow, Poland — The Rigged ATM Exchange (tourist-trap, severity: high). You spot a currency exchange booth or get prompted by an ATM to 'convert to your home currency' — the option looks helpful, but the exchange rate is catastrophic. Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) at Polish ATMs and exchange kiosks in tourist zones can eat 10-20% of your money. Redditors report seeing 'kantor' booths with '0% commission' signs that actually offer terrible rates, especially near the Main Square. How to avoid: Always decline DCC at ATMs — choose to pay in Polish zloty Use Revolut or Wise for cash exchange If using a kantor, check rates at NBP.pl first Avoid exchange booths right next to tourist attractions

Scam alert in Krakow, Poland — The Horse Carriage Price Ambush (transport, severity: moderate). The horse-drawn carriages around the Main Square look charming in all the photos, but tourists consistently report being quoted one price verbally and then handed a bill 3-5x higher at the end of the ride. The driver never clarified whether the price was per person or total, and somehow 'extras' were added. One Redditor reported being charged €120 for what seemed like a €30 ride. How to avoid: Confirm the TOTAL price in writing before you get in Ask if it's per person or for the whole carriage Walk away if they won't show you a price list Book through an official tourism office instead

Scam alert in Krakow, Poland — The Airport Taxi Overcharge (nightlife, severity: moderate). You exit the airport and a driver immediately approaches offering a ride to your hotel. He seems official, even has a jacket. The 'meter' runs mysteriously fast, and you end up paying 3-4x the normal fare. The legitimate fare from the airport to the Old Town should be around 60-80 PLN, but unlicensed drivers regularly charge €30-50+. Redditors warn that the most aggressive touts wait just outside arrivals. How to avoid: Pre-book a taxi via iCar or Bolt from the airport app Use the official MDA (Municipal Transport Authority) taxi stand inside the terminal Agree on price before getting in if you use a street taxi Bolt and Uber are reliable and cheaper

Scam alert in Krakow, Poland — The 'Free' Shot Invitation (nightlife, severity: moderate). A promoter outside a bar hands you a flyer promising a 'free shot' or 'free welcome drink' if you come inside. You go in, the drink arrives — and then the bill for the rest of the evening makes it very clear the 'free' drink was just the hook. Some venues operate on a sliding scale: the more you drink, the more creative the pricing gets. Several Reddit threads document groups being charged €20+ per cocktail with no menu prices. How to avoid: Never accept 'free' drinks from strangers outside clubs Look up bar reviews before going in Always ask for a menu and confirm prices before ordering Stick to reputable venues recommended by your hostel

Scam alert in Krakow, Poland — The Fake Charity Collector (pickpocket, severity: low). Someone approaches you with a clipboard and a vest that looks vaguely official, asking you to sign a petition and 'donate' to a cause — deaf children, homeless animals, earthquake victims. The clipboard is passed around your group and everyone feels social pressure to sign and put money in the envelope. The charity doesn't exist. This is a common pickpocket distraction across Europe and is well-reported in Krakow. How to avoid: Just walk away — you're not obligated to interact Keep your hand on your wallet if anyone approaches in a group Legitimate charities don't solicit in tourist areas this way Say 'nie dziękuję' (no thank you) firmly

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — Euronet ATM Trap (tourist-trap, severity: high). You spot a bright yellow Euronet ATM right on Staroměstské náměstí and think nothing of it — it's just an ATM, right? The machine asks if you want to use 'their' conversion rate instead of your bank's, and without reading carefully, you click confirm. You've just paid a 20% conversion markup on top of a fat withdrawal fee. Back at the hostel in Žižkov, another traveler shows you traveler reports where dozens of tourists describe losing €30–50 in a single ATM visit this way. As one traveler bluntly put it: 'Euronet is a legal scam dressed up in a neon box.' How to avoid: Always decline dynamic currency conversion — choose to be charged in Czech koruna (CZK) Use ATMs attached to actual Czech banks: Česká spořitelna, ČSOB, Komerční banka Withdraw larger amounts less frequently to minimize per-transaction fees Use Revolut, Wise, or Charles Schwab debit cards that waive foreign ATM fees Never use ATMs on Old Town Square or Wenceslas Square — walk two blocks to a bank branch

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — Unlicensed Taxi Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). It's 2am and you've just left a bar on Dlouhá Street when a driver waves you over near the taxi rank on Wenceslas Square. He says 'flat rate, 500 koruna' and you get in. Twenty minutes later he's demanding 2,000 CZK and pointing at a meter that was somehow running the whole time. You recognize the scam from traveler reports — the classic move is either a broken meter, a rigged meter, or simply arguing there's a 'night surcharge.' One traveler lost $100 on a 15-minute ride this way, writing: 'The driver locked the doors until I paid. I should have just used Bolt.' How to avoid: Use Bolt or Uber exclusively in Prague — price is locked in before you get in If you must take a street taxi, only use AAA Radiotaxi (tel: 14014) or Liftago Confirm the price before entering and insist the meter is running from the start Screenshot the route on Google Maps so you can verify the driver isn't taking a detour Never get into a taxi that approaches you — always initiate the booking yourself

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — The Tip Trick at Tourist Restaurants (overcharging, severity: moderate). You settle into a charming restaurant just off the Charles Bridge in Malá Strana and order goulash and a beer. The bill arrives and looks reasonable — until your friend notices the waiter has already added a 15% 'service charge' in small print and is now handing you the card reader with the tip screen defaulted to 20% on top of that. You'd be tipping 35% total. Traveler reports warn about exactly this: some restaurants in the tourist belt stack hidden service charges then guilt-trip you for not tipping further. One traveler noted: 'Compared to Berlin, Prague old town is just a scammy tourist trap with cool architecture.' How to avoid: Always ask for an itemized bill and check every line before paying Look for menus posted outside — if no prices are displayed, walk on Eat two blocks away from major landmarks where locals actually dine If a service charge is already included, it's normal to leave nothing extra or just round up Use Google Maps reviews filtered to 'locals' or look for Czech language reviews

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — Charity Ham / Petition Scam (counterfeit, severity: moderate). You're admiring the Astronomical Clock on Old Town Square when someone approaches holding a clipboard and a sign about deaf children. They ask you to sign a petition and shove the clipboard into your hands. The moment your pen touches paper, they point to the 'donation amount' column and expect a large cash donation — often €20–50. The 'charity' is entirely fake. Traveler reports celebrated when the notorious Old Town Square ham stall shut down — but petition scammers remain. One traveler wrote: 'They count on tourists who don't understand the sign. It's a notorious scam spot right on Old Town Square, a disgrace.' How to avoid: Never take a clipboard from a stranger in a tourist area — just keep walking Say 'ne, díky' (no, thank you in Czech) firmly and don't make eye contact If someone puts a bracelet, flower, or clipboard in your hands, immediately give it back Legitimate charities in Czech Republic don't solicit on tourist squares this way Report persistent scammers to the Prague City Police booth near Old Town Square

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — Currency Exchange Rip-Off (tourist-trap, severity: high). The exchange kiosk on Václavské náměstí is advertising '0% commission!' in enormous letters and you think you've found a deal. You hand over €200 and get back far fewer Czech crowns than expected. The catch: the advertised rate was for selling CZK, not buying it, and the actual buying rate was buried in tiny print. You only realize you've been swindled when you compare rates at the hotel. Multiple traveler reports confirm these kiosks are considered a citywide embarrassment — one traveler posted: 'PLEASE!! In Czech Republic, honest ATMs at banks WON'T ever give you EUROS. Our currency is Czech koruna — these exchange offices are preying on confused tourists.' How to avoid: Use ATMs at Czech bank branches (Česká spořitelna, ČSOB) and decline conversion If you must exchange cash, use the post office (Česká pošta) or a bank branch inside Always calculate the final amount you should receive before handing over money The official rate is roughly 24–25 CZK per euro — anything below 22 is a rip-off Apps like XE.com show live mid-market rates — screenshot it and compare

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — Strip Club Drink Scam (nightlife, severity: high). A friendly local-looking woman near Wenceslas Square strikes up a conversation and suggests a 'nice local bar' nearby. You have a few drinks, she orders what seem like regular cocktails, and when the bill arrives it's €400 for six drinks. The bar has a bouncer blocking the door. The menu she ordered from had prices ten times higher than the regular menu you were shown — a version sold specifically to tourists dragged in by 'bar girls' on commission. One traveler described this as 'the most aggressive scam I've encountered in Europe — they had three bouncers and I had to call the police to leave.' How to avoid: Never follow strangers who approach you on the street to a bar they recommend Always check a menu with prices before sitting down — walk out if they refuse to show it If trapped, calmly photograph the menu and your bill, then call the police (158) Stick to bars on TripAdvisor or Google Maps with verifiable recent reviews Travel with at least one other person when exploring Wenceslas Square nightlife

Scam alert in Prague, Czech Republic — Fake E-Bike Tour Operators (transport, severity: moderate). You rent a fat e-bike from a stand near Old Town Square that promises a 'self-guided city tour.' The operator never mentions that in Prague, riding e-bikes with motors above a certain wattage on public roads without a driver's license is illegal. When police stop you on the embankment near Nusle Bridge, you're facing a fine equivalent to hundreds of euros — and the rental operator is nowhere to be found. Traveler reports have exposed the practice: the operators know the rules but deliberately don't inform tourists, collecting rent fees while tourists absorb all legal risk. How to avoid: Only rent from established operators with verified Google reviews and a physical storefront Ask explicitly: 'Do I need a driver's license for this bike?' — if hesitation, walk away Stick to pedal-assist bikes (pedelecs) under 25km/h which don't require a license Prague Bikes and Praha Bike are reputable licensed tour operators If stopped by police while renting legally, the rental contract should show the operator's liability

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Ferry Port 'Predator' Taxi Overcharge (overcharging, severity: high). A ring of unlicensed 'private taxi' drivers works the Split ferry terminal with laminated €20-per-kilometre rate cards. Three documented Croatian-press case files: two Italian women charged €550 for a 25-km ferry-to-airport run in August 2024 (Sarajevo Times, Aug 26); €643 for the short ride from the ferry port to the Čiovo bridge in July 2025, driver quoted 'Split glavno mesto' as justification (24ur.com); €201 for a 10-minute agreed-€21 ride (Tripadvisor 'Taxi scam in Split - Beware'). Transport Minister Oleg Butković announced on Nova TV Dnevnik (Aug 28, 2025) that the government would reintroduce maximum fare limits specifically in response to Split and Dubrovnik cases (Croatia Week). Traveler reports explain the loophole: Croatian taxi law permits a driver to set any price as long as a price list is visibly posted in the vehicle. Legitimate operators: Yellow Taxi Split, Cammeo, Bolt, Uber. How to avoid: Open Uber, Bolt, or Cammeo before you leave the ferry; fares are shown in-app before confirming. Walk two minutes to the bus station on Obala Lazareta — Pleso Prijevoz €8 to SPU airport, €2 to Old Town, €3 to Kaštela. Call Yellow Taxi Split on +385 21 345 678 for a metered local ride. Photograph the plate and driver's ID before loading luggage; insist on the meter. Report overcharges to +385 21 307 111 (Split-Dalmatia Police) within 48 hours with the plate number. Scam alert in Split, Croatia — SPU Airport & Kaštela Taxi Overcharge (overcharging, severity: high). Split Airport (SPU) sits 25 km from the Old Town in Kaštel Štafilić, a distance long enough that taxi fares can be padded significantly. Total Croatia News (May 11, 2023) documented an illegal driver charging 900 kuna (€120) for a Radisson Blu Hotel to SPU run that legitimate operators priced at 300 kuna (€40); a Tripadvisor review of Airport Taxi J.d.o.o. (Kaštel Lukšić) logs HRK 260 (€35) for a 6.5-km SPU-to-Seget transfer. Traveler reports warn: 'They will try to charge you 600 kn from airport to city. Its toooo much.' Rick Steves Split forum: a legitimate metered SPU-to-Split-center ride is about €50. The mechanic combines distance (SPU is far enough that honest rides are €35–50) plus the same 'private taxi with posted price list' loophole as the ferry-port scam. Pressure peaks during Ultra Europe (second weekend of July, 150,000 festival-goers) with surge-priced return rides. How to avoid: Take the Pleso Prijevoz airport bus (€8 single) to the Split bus station, then walk 15 minutes to the Riva. Local Promet Split bus 37 also links SPU to the bus station for about €3. Open Uber, Bolt, or Cammeo (+385 1 1212) before leaving the terminal — fares shown in-app. Use Yellow Taxi Split +385 21 345 678 for metered local rides. Photograph the plate and confirm the meter reads zero before the ride starts. For Ultra Europe returns, pre-book via Pleso Prijevoz or a registered transfer operator to avoid surge. For overcharges, call 112 or Split-Dalmatia Police +385 21 307 111 and Split Tourist Board +385 21 348 600.

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Riva Promenade & Old Town Menu Trap (overcharging, severity: moderate). Riva-promenade cafés charge €5–7 for a coffee that costs €2 three streets inland. Tripadvisor 'Old Split: Overrated prices, scammers and poor service' has been one of the most-upvoted Split Tripadvisor reviews since 2016; 'Disgrace' (Riva Harbor, Jul 1, 2019) documents the Riva-side version. Traveler reports give the local filter: 'All restaurants will have 4+ stars on google review. If its lower than 4.5 its a potential warning sign.' Broader traveler pricing complaints note: 'Split, Hvar, Brac, Dubrovnik, Zadar... south of Zadar are scam level prices, more expensive than London and NYC.' Three Split-specific moves: Riva-side café pricing (€5–7 coffee, €8–10 beer, €15 basic pizza); Peristyle cafés at €10 spritz and €8 coffee sold on the drama of Roman stones; and seafood 'market rate by the kilogram' with weight and per-kg price undisclosed until the bill arrives. How to avoid: Eat off the Riva — Varoš, Bačvice (non-club side), the residential alleys off Marmontova. Good options: Villa Spiza (Petra Krešimira IV), Konoba Matejuska (Tomića Stine 3), Bokeria (Domaldova 8) — all Google-reviewed at 4.5+ stars with recent reviews. Ask for the printed English menu with prices before you order; photograph the chalkboard. For fish, confirm price per kilogram and total in euros before it goes to the grill. Pay by card for chargeback; retain the receipt with business registration number. For disputes, call 072 213 213 (Ministry of Finance), +385 21 307 111 (Split-Dalmatia Police), or +385 21 348 600 (Split Tourist Board).

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Bacvice 'Gentlemen's Club' Bill Trap (overcharging, severity: high). Boss Club Split and the wider Bačvice / Old Town strip-club cluster have run a consistent bill-trap for years. A Jul 18, 2025 Tripadvisor review ('Criminal scam – avoid at all costs') describes a €260 bill for '2 drinks + 2 Private dances' never consented to, with women making physical contact 'to get attention.' A Jun 30, 2025 review lays out the credit-card side: a vodka Red Bull initially quoted at €20 was rung up at €30, with private-room charges of ~€100 and ~€190 stacked as separate transactions. A 2017 traveler thread on Slomljeno Srce Noćni klub warned: 'Never go to any strip clubs in Central or Eastern Europe, it is literally scam-central.' Three-stage mechanic: promoters on Marmontova, the Riva, or Bačvice boardwalk after midnight offer 'free entry' or 'VIP wristband'; inside, €20 cover plus two young women order champagne at €100+ per bottle; final bill is €300–2,000 with bouncer blocking exit until card is run. Cruise stopovers, bachelor parties, and Ultra Europe crowds are primary targets. How to avoid: Refuse every promoter approach on Marmontova, the Riva, or Bačvice after midnight — any stranger offering 'free entry' is a commission-paid recruiter. Choose Split nightlife only at well-reviewed venues with printed menus (Central Club Split, Vanilla, Inbox). Never let your card leave your sight; photograph receipts before signing or entering a PIN. If physically blocked, call 112 or Split-Dalmatia Police +385 21 307 111 immediately. Dispute any 'different amount' or 'services not provided' charge with your card issuer within 30 days (chargeback category: amount different from authorized). File a consumer-protection complaint via Croatian Ministry of Finance 072 213 213 and Split Tourist Board +385 21 348 600.

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Diocletian's Palace 'Legionary' Photo Fee & Unofficial Guide (tourist-trap, severity: moderate). Men dressed as Roman legionaries pose in the Peristyle of Diocletian's Palace and initiate selfies with tourists, then demand €5–20 per photo — alongside unlicensed 'Game of Thrones' and 'Diocletian' tour guides touting at Iron Gate without the Ministry of Tourism badge that Croatian law requires. The Croatia Travel Facebook group's 2024 post 'Scam Alert: Legionaries in Split, Croatia Targeting Tourists' is the primary community warning; the pattern echoes Rome's Colosseum gladiators and Barcelona's Las Ramblas statues. Two-move opener on the Peristyle: a legionary in plastic armour and red plume offers to pose with you holding a sword near the sphinx at the south side or on the Cathedral steps; the first photo is free, the second and the group photo are not. A confederate materialises with a card reader or a laminated 'CONTRIBUTION €20' card. Unlicensed-guide variant works Iron Gate (Željezna Vrata) at Narodni Trg and Silver Gate (Srebrna Vrata), offering 'hourly Diocletian tours' or 'Game of Thrones walking tours' at €10–20 per person without a visible license badge. How to avoid: Do not pose for photos with anyone in costume inside the Peristyle or on the Cathedral steps unless a price is agreed in writing — in practice, decline the approach. For guided tours, any legitimate tour guide in Split must wear a visible Ministry of Tourism badge with a license number — ask to see it before agreeing to pay; cross-check against the Split Tourist Board's licensed-guide list at +385 21 348 600. Book tours through Split Tourist Board, named agencies (Secret Dalmatia, Split Walking Tours, Maestral Travel Agency), or a major OTA with 500+ reviews. Hrvatska Turistička Policija run summer patrols in the Palace — call 112 or +385 21 307 111 if a costumed/unlicensed operator refuses to leave you alone. For losses paid, file with Ministry of Finance 072 213 213 and Split Tourist Board.

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Jadrolinija & Krilo Ferry Ticket Tout (overcharging, severity: moderate). The official Jadrolinija foot-passenger Split–Hvar ferry is €8.36 high season (€5.84 low) and the Krilo catamaran Split–Hvar is €8–15, but touts and third-party sites sell the same ticket at €20–30. Tripadvisor's Jadrolinija Split page carries 522 reviews with recurring 'Scam' headlines ('Avoid Jadrolinija at all costs'). The Hvar Croatia Travel Facebook 'Scam warning at Split ferry port' post (2024) combines the ferry-tout pattern with the taxi one. Three tiers: unmarked kiosks along Obala kneza Domagoja sell real tickets with €5–10 markup (legal but avoidable); third-party sites like 'ferry-split-hvar.com' add reservation/service/insurance fees until the €8 ticket is €30; and occasional phishing domains mimicking jadrolinija.hr that sell tickets which don't scan at the pier. A related scam: pre-paid 'ferry + taxi combo' where the ferry works but the 'guaranteed taxi' is unlicensed and charges a premium at the destination. How to avoid: Buy Jadrolinija tickets at jadrolinija.hr or the terminal counter (Split–Hvar foot passenger €8.36). Buy Krilo catamaran tickets at krilo.hr or the Kapetan Luka counter (Split–Hvar from €8). Avoid pop-up kiosks on Obala kneza Domagoja unless you confirm the ticket is issued by Jadrolinija or Krilo with a visible company logo and printed fare matching the official rate. For OTAs, use only Klook, Direct Ferries, Ferryhopper, or GetYourGuide with 1,000+ reviews. Do not pre-pay a 'ferry + taxi + lunch' street package. For disputes, call Jadrolinija customer service +385 21 338 333 or Krilo +385 21 645 476; Split Tourist Board +385 21 348 600; Ministry of Finance 072 213 213.

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Old Town & Ferry Terminal Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: moderate). The US State Department rates pickpocketing as the principal crime risk in Croatia and the UK FCDO names Split directly as a location where 'pickpockets operate in tourist areas.' Travelsafe-Abroad flags Split's ferry terminals specifically as 'medium risk.' Real hotspots: narrow lanes inside Diocletian's Palace (Dioklecijanova 2–3 metres wide), the Peškarija fish market mid-morning tour crush, and the Gat Svetog Duje arrival — a 1,200-passenger ferry disembarking onto a narrow pier with queueing taxis, luggage carts, and local commuters intersecting for five minutes. Tripadvisor's 'Beautiful narrow streets, be aware of pickpockets though' Old Split review: 'Be aware of the pickpockets, we experienced it twice.' The Riva at early evening is more open, but a phone pulled out for a sunset photo is visible from ten metres; a confederate can bump the shoulder while a partner lifts. Unlike Barcelona La Rambla teams, Split operations tend to be opportunistic rather than organized-group, so vigilance at three or four specific compression points handles most of the risk. How to avoid: Wear bags crossbody with the zipper against your chest; keep phone in a zipped front pocket, never a back pocket or the outer mesh pouch of a backpack. Inside Diocletian's Palace, briefly turn your backpack to your front as you enter the narrower lanes (Dioklecijanova north of the Peristyle); do the same at the Peškarija and Pazar during the mid-morning tour-group wave. At the Gat Svetog Duje ferry arrival, stay at your luggage until the crowd thins. On the Riva at sunset, keep the phone off the stone bench. Carry only one card and €100–200 cash; leave the rest in the apartment safe. For thefts, call 112 or 192 (Police) and file at Split-Dalmatia Police +385 21 307 111. Split Tourist Board +385 21 348 600 has a walk-in desk for incident-report referrals.

Scam alert in Split, Croatia — Split Apartment Booking.com Fraud & Fake Listing (identity-theft, severity: high). The Polish embassy in Zagreb issued a 2024 warning to Polish tourists booking Split and other Dalmatian accommodations on Booking.com: 'Scammers operate by publishing an offer for the same accommodation several times at different prices, leading to overbooking' (TVP World, 2024; Zagreb.info). The BBC's Nov 2024 'reservation hijacking' story documents the second mechanic: a data breach leaked guest bookings to criminals who send WhatsApp messages impersonating the hotel and asking for 'card verification.' A 2021 Tripadvisor review 'Was Split Centre Apartments & Booking.com Complicit in Scam' documents a specific Split case; a 2024 traveler PSA on Booking.com Croatia confirms the phishing-website pattern. A splitcroatiatravel Facebook 2024 post describes a specific fake listing with five positive reviews and one older warning stating 'the property isn't real.' Three versions: cloned listing (scammer copies a real Split apartment, takes €500–1,500 SEPA and disappears); reservation-hijack (WhatsApp credential phish after legitimate Booking.com booking); and overbooking (same apartment listed three or four times at different prices, first tourist through the door keeps it). How to avoid: Book only through the official Booking.com, Airbnb, or Vrbo app — never through an email link — and ignore any request for card verification or payment outside the platform. Pay only on arrival, keys in hand. Cross-check the property in the Croatian eVisitor tourism registry and the host at sudreg.pravosudje.hr (both free). Use a credit card with chargeback rights; never pay by SEPA before arrival. For losses, call Split-Dalmatia Police on 112 or +385 21 307 111 and file a chargeback within 30 days. US Embassy Zagreb +385 1 661 2200, UK Embassy Zagreb +385 1 6009 100 for emergency accommodation referrals. Croatian Ombudsman +385 1 49 21 837 and Split Tourist Board +385 21 348 600 for consumer complaints.
